app.title: Agile Quiz
app.tagline: A quick quiz on Scrum, Kanban, and agile practice.

s.label: Grade S · Scrum Master vibes
s.tip: Perfect score! You can facilitate the next retrospective — just keep the timebox.

a.label: Grade A · Close to the Sprint Goal
a.tip: So close. Drop that miss into the backlog and review it next round.

b.label: Grade B · Ready for Daily Scrum
b.tip: Solid middle ground — like a standup that ends on time. Synced, with room to go deeper.

c.label: Grade C · Needs refinement first
c.tip: Concepts are a bit fuzzy. Grab a user-story card and write clear acceptance criteria.

d.label: Grade D · Read the Scrum Guide first
d.tip: No worries — agile is a practice sport. Play again, and start with who owns the value.

q1.prompt: In Scrum, what does a “Sprint” usually mean?
q1.a: An emergency hotfix window after a production release
q1.b: A fixed-length iteration that can produce a usable increment
q1.c: A few overtime days the team sprints to ship
q1.d: A yearly milestone on the product roadmap
q1.funFact: Sprints are typically 1–4 weeks; keeping the length stable helps the team forecast.

q2.prompt: What is the main purpose of the Daily Scrum?
q2.a: Report to a manager how many hours everyone worked yesterday
q2.b: Assign every task for the next Sprint on the spot
q2.c: Let developers sync progress, surface blockers, and adjust the day’s plan
q2.d: Have the Product Owner demo new features to customers
q2.funFact: The classic three questions are just a common format — the point is developer alignment, not status theater.

q3.prompt: What problem does a “Definition of Done” mainly solve?
q3.a: Agreeing what “done” means so the increment is truly usable
q3.b: Requiring a fixed number of lines of code per person per day
q3.c: Defining when the Product Owner may change requirements
q3.d: Listing rules that ban time off during a Sprint
q3.funFact: Without a shared DoD, teams often mistake “code written” for “ready to release.”

q4.prompt: What is the Product Owner’s core responsibility?
q4.a: Assign daily tasks and micromanage progress
q4.b: Manage the Product Backlog to maximize product value
q4.c: Build the CI/CD pipeline and run the servers
q4.funFact: The PO owns what to build and in what order; the developers own how to build it.

q5.prompt: What usually makes a good user story?
q5.a: Only technical implementation details, no business goal
q5.b: The longer the better — pack half a year of work into one card
q5.c: Describe role, goal, and value, with verifiable acceptance criteria
q5.d: Must be written only by QA; developers cannot contribute
q5.funFact: A common template is “As a… I want… so that…”. INVEST is often used to check story quality.

q6.prompt: What is a Sprint Retrospective mainly for?
q6.a: Demo this Sprint’s increment to leadership
q6.b: Estimate story points for the next Sprint
q6.c: Check whether code coverage hit the target
q6.d: Reflect on how the team works and commit to improvements
q6.funFact: Retrospectives focus on people and process; Sprint Review focuses more on the product increment.

q7.prompt: In agile, what does “velocity” usually mean?
q7.a: Peak requests per second the servers can handle
q7.b: A reference pace for how much work a team finishes across Sprints
q7.c: How fast daily active users grow after launch
q7.d: Average time spent in code review
q7.funFact: Velocity is for forecasting, not for ranking teams — that race often inflates story points.

q8.prompt: In Kanban, what is the main benefit of limiting WIP?
q8.a: Force everyone to start more tasks so they look busy
q8.b: Reduce context switching, expose bottlenecks, and improve flow
q8.c: Keep the board forever at exactly three columns
q8.d: Remove all priorities so whoever finishes first picks next
q8.funFact: Finish more by starting less: WIP limits are a core lever for Kanban throughput.

q9.prompt: What does Product Backlog refinement usually involve?
q9.a: Clarify fuzzy items and acceptance criteria to prepare for upcoming Sprints
q9.b: Change requirements urgently on release day
q9.c: Delete every user story that has not started
q9.d: Assign development tasks directly to individuals
q9.funFact: Refinement is ongoing — you should not see a story for the first time only in Sprint Planning.

q10.prompt: What does an MVP (Minimum Viable Product) emphasize?
q10.a: Ship as many features as possible and polish everything first
q10.b: Validate core assumptions with the least effort and get feedback early
q10.c: Must use microservices and a cloud-native stack
q10.d: Polish the UI first and leave business logic for later
q10.funFact: “Minimum” is about learning fast — not about delivering half-baked work just to check a box.
